1:
That the opening is ironic nobody doubts, though Gill arrives there by eliminating the alternative. The phrase could mean that they were merely of the common people, ignorant for all their dictating; but since Job goes on to compare himself with them and to deny that he falls below them, the words must grant them some standing, and so expose their self-conceit. Clarke says it in a line, that all wisdom is concentrated in them and when they die there will be none left, and calls it a strong irony. Henry hears a claim to the monopoly of wisdom, that the world must be in the dark when their sun has set; and he thinks Job may be turning back Zophar's comparison of him to the wild ass's colt, as if to say that we must be asses and you are the only men. Henry and Wesley then draw the same consolation in almost the same words, that when wise and good men die it is a comfort to think wisdom and goodness do not die with them, since God has the residue of the Spirit and can raise up others more fit to do his work.

On Job's counter-claim the witnesses split between the lexical and the moral. Gill notes the marginal reading, that Job says he has a heart as well as they, and expands it into a natural understanding and a spiritual one that knows the living Redeemer who should stand on the earth in the latter day. Clarke turns it against the friends: their boasted wisdom consists only in strings of proverbs which are in every person's mouth and prove nothing in those who use them. Wesley makes the same point, that neither side has reason to be puffed up, since the most barbarous nations know God to be infinite in wisdom, but that this is not the question between them. Henry reads the claim as said to humble them rather than to magnify himself, and draws a rule from it, that those we contend with have a capacity and a right of judging too, and may be in the right while we are in the wrong.

The verse about being mocked is the chapter's hardest, and Clarke says so outright: it is very difficult, and no two critics seem to be agreed. He lays three renderings side by side, Good's, Coverdale's and Parkhurst's, and closes by observing that to emendations and conjectures there is no end. Ellicott narrows the ambiguity to one question, whether this is the character Job claims for himself or the supposed taunt of his friends, and adds the judgment that ridicule is no test of truth or of merit. Gill notes an alternative from Sephorno but prefers to read Job as instancing himself as proof that good men are afflicted. Henry alone doubts the charge, warning that we are apt to call reproofs reproaches and to think ourselves mocked when we are only admonished.

At the lamp Ellicott is blunt that the English rendering conveys no sense, and offers two constructions, one making the torch prepared for tottering feet the thing disregarded, the other and likelier making contempt for calamity the thing that lies ready in the thoughts of the man at ease. Henry supplies the image the verse wants, that a lamp taken out of its golden candlestick and put into an earthen pitcher is valued by nobody as before. On the prosperity of robbers Gill names the Chaldeans and Sabeans who had plundered Job himself, and grants the fact cannot be denied and has been a trial to good men. Clarke accepts the difficulty and refuses the inference: these are administrations of providence which cannot be accounted for, yet the Judge of all the earth does right, and therefore prosperity and adversity are no evidence of a man's spiritual state.
7:
What the beasts teach divides the witnesses more sharply than the invitation suggests. Gill makes the lesson a hard one and specifies it: the creatures most harmless and useful are the ones that fall prey, sheep and lambs to lions and wolves, doves to hawks, the lesser fish to the greater, so that nature itself shows the righteous afflicted and the wicked prospering. Wesley takes the appeal as a rebuke of method: what Zophar had uttered with so much pomp and gravity about God's infinite wisdom needs no journey into heaven or hell, being learnable from the beasts. Clarke gives most of his space to Good's paraphrase, which makes Job answer that this is the common doctrine of all nature, but that to apply it as the friends apply it, and infer that he suffers for hypocrisy, is impertinent, since why good and evil are promiscuously scattered through nature and human life they are as ignorant of as he. Gill adds the vegetable witness, that a sprig of the earth unites in the doctrine that it is raised and preserved by God.

At the ninth verse two witnesses notice the same rarity. Ellicott observes that this is the only place in the dialogue parts of the book where the sacred name of Jehovah appears, that no one of the friends ever uses it, and that Job's use of it in such a context is the clearest evidence of the superior knowledge he claims. Wesley records the same fact, adding that God in that age was more known by the name Shaddai, the Almighty. Over the following verse Clarke works on the two Hebrew terms, the soul of all life and the breath of all flesh, and asks whether the first does not refer to the immortal soul, and the second to respiration, the means of animal life. Gill keeps the point providential, that two sparrows are not worth a farthing and not one falls to the ground without the knowledge and will of God.

The ear and the palate are read by everyone as a rule of discrimination, and the question is whom the rule is aimed at. Delitzsch states it flatly: the sayings of the ancients are not to be accepted without being proved. Ellicott makes the target Bildad, who had appealed to the wisdom of authority and tradition, and he allows that wisdom is the prerogative of age, then turns the concession, since on that principle the Ancient of Days must needs be wise indeed. Clarke makes the target the friends in general: these are all common-place sayings, they have advanced nothing new and cast no light on the dispensations of providence. Wesley alone takes the line as a preface rather than a rebuke, an invitation to hear and judge his words candidly.

On the wisdom of the ancients Gill canvasses four readings before settling: that Job means himself, which is how some think Eliphaz took him; that he is wishing some ancient man would judge the case between them; that he is answering Bildad's advice to search the fathers, allowing their wisdom but only so far as it agrees with the wisdom of God; or, as Gill thinks best, that the words are a proverb generally agreed to, that men advanced in years have usually learned much by observation and experience. Clarke supplies a historical reason for the proverb, that men living in primitive times, when the creation and the fall and the flood and the confusion of tongues were recent facts, and that their length of days let them accumulate so much wisdom by experience that they are deservedly considered as oracles. Wesley reads the verse as a concession to Bildad with a reservation attached, that such wisdom is imperfect, mere ignorance if compared with the divine, and that antiquity ought therefore not to be received against the truths of the most wise God.
13:
The hymn opens and closes on the same pair of words, and the witnesses differ on whether the repetition means anything. Gill registers it and lets it stand, the second instance using different words for the same things. Wesley gives it a function, that the formula is repeated to prepare the way for the instances which follow. Clarke insists the two are not the same at all: the first pairs intelligence with fortitude, which is strength in action, while the second pairs strength with sufficiency, power in essence and an eternal potentiality. With him is every excellence, Clarke concludes, in potentia and in esse, and as he is self-existent so is he self-sufficient.

On the breaking down that cannot be repaired Clarke reaches for an argument from physics before one from history. God alone can create and God alone can destroy; no skill or cunning of man can annihilate the smallest particle of matter, for man may change its form by chemical agency, but to reduce it to nothing belongs to God alone. Only then does he name the political instances, Nineveh and Babylon and Persepolis and Tyre, broken down never to be rebuilt. Gill works instead at identifying the referent, rejecting the tower of Babel because its builders desisted without the tower being broken down, preferring Sodom with Sephorno as an utter and perpetual desolation never rebuilt to this day. Ellicott compresses the whole verse into a sentence, that God has equal power over the moral and the physical world.

At the waters Clarke hears two allusions in one verse, the withholding being the third day's work when the waters were gathered and the dry land appeared, and the sending out being the flood. Wesley reads the first clause of the waters reserved in the clouds and the second of springs and rivers, and agrees that the deluge is manifestly in view. Gill keeps all three open, the gathering at the creation, the retreat after the flood, and the withholding of rain so that even the brook Cherith dried up. The deceived and the deceiver draw the chapter's one properly theological exchange. Clarke reports the reading that refers it to the fall, the beguiler and the beguiled alike belonging to God, and presses the point that the tempter cannot act without express permission. Wesley states the guard that the doctrine needs: God governs the deceiver and sets bounds to his deceits, overruling them to his own glory, yet God is not the author of any error or sin but only the wise and holy governor of it.

In the dismantling of the great the comments are particular. Gill reads the spoiling of counsellors as God confounding their schemes and carrying their counsel headlong. Clarke asks whether the infatuating of judges points to the conduct of some of the Israelitish judges, such as Samson. On the loosing of the bond Gill offers two senses, the yoke kings bind on their subjects being loosed from the subjects, or the king's own waistband being ungirded, which is to unking him; Ellicott makes it the confederacy by which kings bind themselves together, loosed so that they are girded to fight against each other; and Wesley explains the girding from the custom by which servants gathered up their long garments for attendance. Whether the next verse speaks of princes or of priests is left open, Gill reporting the Greek rendering that leads the priests away captive and Ellicott judging that the parallelism suits princes better. Ellicott reads the passage as a whole: it re-echoes the sentiments of Eliphaz but refuses his optimism, Eliphaz being quite sure he holds the key to providence while Job fears his ignorance amounts almost to hopelessness; and Job's breadth of view nonetheless exceeds his friend's, since Eliphaz generalises vaguely while Job declares that not men but nations are the subjects of God's guiding providence.
20:
On the removing of speech Clarke quotes the tag that God infatuates those whom he is determined to destroy, and observes that the elders, for all their wisdom, can do no more to save a state God designs to ruin than a child who can neither reason nor speak. Gill takes the verse as the withdrawal of a gift, and lists the ways it is withdrawn: at death, since the state of the dead is a state of silence; by striking dumb, as Zechariah was struck; by confusion, as at Babel, where one speech was taken away and another given; and by constraint, as Balaam would willingly have cursed Israel and could not.

On the pouring of contempt Gill spends his space on who is not meant. Not good princes who rule in righteousness; nor princes in the figurative sense, the children of God; but bad princes who oppress their subjects and persecute good men, among whom he names Herod and Pontius Pilate, the Roman emperors and the papacy. Clarke works instead on the words. The term here means those of royal extraction, and is quite different from the one in the previous verse; and the clause rendered weakening the strength of the mighty is more properly the loosing of a girdle, the noun meaning the compact, the nervous and sinewy. From that he ventures a reference to the crocodile, and sets out the creature's armour of fifty-two parallel girdles of square scales; against which, he asks, what is human strength, since he alone can loose the girdles of this mighty one.

The deep things brought out of darkness are read three ways that do not meet. Gill makes them the deep things of God, the thoughts of his heart and the decrees he has purposed in himself, hid in darkness until the accomplishment of them discovers them. Clarke offers two other senses, God's works in the great deep, or the plots and stratagems of wicked men, conspiracies deeply laid and about to be produced into existence when death glutted himself with carnage. On the increase and destruction of nations Gill assembles a history, the world peopled before the flood and destroyed at it, Sephorno's reading of the seven nations of Canaan destroyed to make way for Israel, and after them the four monarchies. Clarke follows Good in rendering the clause that God lets the nations grow licentious, and supplies the mechanism: pride and fullness of bread with extensive trade produce luxury, luxury brings profligacy of manners, and when that cup is full God brings against them a nation less pampered and inured to toil.

Ellicott makes the passage the key to much of the history of the world, framed as two questions. Why are nations marked with such characteristic differences, the Greeks and the Romans and the Jews of old, the French and the English and the Germans now? And why does the counsel of the wisest sometimes fail, as with Ahitophel, and the bravery of the boldest forsake them? Because there is One working underneath it all for his own ends. Zophar, with all his common sense, had scarcely risen to this, being prepared to imply that the dealings of God were intelligible, where Job declared them inscrutable and so, from their very darkness, suggestive of the necessity for faith. Ellicott concedes the teaching may seem to savour of fatalism, and answers that Job deals with one side of the problem only; had he found occasion he would have stated the correlative truth of man's absolute responsibility, even though man be but as clay in the potter's hands, since otherwise how should God judge the world. Job's conception of the righteous government of God as far transcended that of his friends as their estimate of his righteousness fell short of the truth, and he is therefore just in saying that he is not inferior to them.
